To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Ca and lidocaine interact with Na channels in a manner that is different from that of the ordinary fast inactivation process.

(1) Na channels can be inactivated by membrane depolarization in the absence of Ca; (2) Na channel SI can be induced by external Ca; (3) lidocaine-induced Na channel blockade can be reversed by external Ca.

(1) Ca-sensitive slow inactivation of Na channels is characterized by 100-ms time constants and incomplete inactivation; (2) Na channel slow inactivation is a direct process, bypassing the open state; (3) the lidocaine-bound state of Na channel is a slow reactivatable state, which is distinct from the fast-inactivated state.
In summary, our research is concerned with
two novel aspects of Na channel gating: Ca-sensitive SI and lidocaine block of Na channels.
the mechanisms of Na channel slow inactivation and its modulation by lidocaine.
the mechanisms of Ca-sensitive slow inactivation, lidocaine block, and the interaction of lidocaine and Ca ions in rat cardiac cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Ca-sensitive SI of cardiac Na channels involves a transition from the resting to a slow inactivation state, bypassing open and ordinary fast inactivated states.
the SI state is not a simple inactivation state but rather a complex state with multiple substates.
Ca-sensitive SI is a separate state, which is distinct from the ordinary fast inactivation and is not associated with the O state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
lidocaine and Ca ions compete in their interaction with Na channels.
Ca-sensitive slow inactivation of Na channels is due to a transition of the Na channel from the R state to the Y state, and that the Y state is a new inactivation state.

Ca-sensitive SI of Na channels in rat cardiac myocytes is due to the presence of a new Y state, and lidocaine interaction slows reactivation of Na channels through interaction with the lidocaine-bound Y state.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SI state of Na channels is a separate state, distinct from the I state, and that Ca and lidocaine can modulate the probability of Na channels entering the SI state.
Ca ions modulate Na channel gating and block by local anesthetics in cardiac cells.
